newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore slowdown unlikely election factor.
newsitem.headline: Singapore slowdown unlikely election factor.

text.p: Singapore's economic slowdown is unlikely to spoil an otherwise assured win for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) in a general election expected this year, economists said on Thursday.
"So long as the economy does not get into a serious depression, there should not be any resentment vote," said Sy Jian, a director at Rashid Hussain Cathay Research.
"A serious recession appears unlikely at this point of time."

The government last month dropped its 1996 growth foreast to between seven and eight percent from an earlier prediction of between 7.5 and 8.5 percent, largely on account of slower growth in electronic exports.
Most analysts have cut their forecasts too, with predictions now ranging from seven to 7.6 percent. In 1995, the Singapore economy grew 8.9 percent.
The next general election must be held by April 1997 -- the year when economists predict the economy will grow between six and eight percent.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said recently there would be no poll before November. In the last election in 1991, the PAP won 77 seats in the 81-member parliament, conceding just four seats to the opposition.
That win, although overwhelming, nevertheless represented the worst performance in more than 20 years for the PAP, which has ruled the prosperous island state since 1959.

Goh, who staked his reputation on bettering the 63 percent of the vote for the PAP that his predecessor Lee Kuan Yew achieved at the 1988 election, was disappointed when his party garnered 61 percent.
He said last week that, given his six-year track record, he expected to do better this time.
Economists told Reuters that while economic growth was unlikely to be a major factor, specific issues could be.
They said the high costs of cars, flats and medical care were issues that might affect the PAP's voting margin.
Maminder Singh, economist at Nomura Research, said the government's economic track record had been good and the people were likely to vote for it.
"Apart from the current slowdown, the overall economy has been healthy as seen in the past economic growth and rising income of the people," he said
The economy has grown by an average of nine to 10 percent since Singapore came out of the recession in 1986-87.

Mukul Asher, associate professor of economics and public policy at National University of Singapore, said it was hard to say how much the slowdown would be a factor because a seven percent projected rate of growth for 1996 was still good.
"So, it will now depend how voters perceive their wellbeing and future prospects. There is probably some room for greater assurance to voters on these aspects," Asher said.

"At the present moment, we are not talking about a recession but about a temporary and modest slowing down in growth to seven percent this year," said Paul Schymyck, chief regional economist (Asia-Pacific) at the Canadian Imperical Bank of Commerce.
The situation was not so bad as to warrant government intervention. "I don't think it is linked to any political issue or likely to have an impact on elections," he said.
"The seven percent projected growth is widely regarded as the upper end of Singapore's long-term sustainable growth of between five and seven percent," Schymyck said.
"This shows Singapore is doing fine," he added.
